title: Your chain
hookLine: you're now a link in the chain
tomorrow: Amira's days are chaos. what did monks and Muslims both write down?

cards: A card in crayon: thank you teacher, with a drawing of a cat that might be a horse. A small piece of paper, carrying a lot. And a second later, a stranger thought arrives: who taught me?
Who's owed one of these cards from me, and never got it? Muslims have a word for the line of people standing behind what you know.

teach.b: The word is isnad: the chain. A hadith comes with one. This person heard it from that person, who heard it from another, back to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ.

Hadith scholars checked the links: was this narrator honest, careful, did he actually meet the one before him? 'Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, quoted in the introduction to Sahih Muslim, said the chain is part of the religion; without it, anyone could say whatever they liked.
Now turn that around, toward your own life.
Your faith, or your love of anything, has a chain too, just never written down. The person who taught you al-Fatiha. The one who fixed your wudu without making you feel small.
The aunt who answered the question you were scared to ask. And now you're a link yourself, the one a kid hands a crayon card to. The tradition ties thanks to that chain.
A hadith in Sunan Abu Dawud says that whoever does not thank people has not thanked God.
Knowledge moves down the chain. Thanks is meant to move back up it. One to tell a friend tonight: a hadith's chain is a list of students who became teachers.

how: Students of hadith and of Qur'an recitation may receive an ijaza, a license naming their chain of teachers; in some circles students pray for their teachers by name.

o: the family tree that proves a noble line of descent
the teachers behind what you know, with you as the next
a string of prayer beads handed down in a family

p: the chain of narrators behind a hadith
the chain is part of the religion
thank people, and you thank God

s: a hadith's isnad is the list of people who passed it on
this person heard it from that one, back to the Prophet.
the chain was a formality nobody checked
hadith scholars checked each narrator: honest, careful, and did they really meet?
thanking people is separate from thanking God
Abu Dawud: whoever does not thank people has not thanked God.

games.q: you got your first job through a mentor who has since moved away. at your promotion dinner, you get to say a few words. what fits 'a link in the chain'?
o: thank the boss in the room. thanks belongs to whoever signs off now.
name the mentor who started you, and the team that carried you.
keep it about the work. naming people turns it into a speech.
games.why: knowledge came down a chain of people, and the hadith says thanking people is part of thanking God. the mentor is a link, even far away.

practice: Choose one teacher in your chain: a parent, a coach, a weekend-school teacher, whoever showed you something that stuck. Write them a two-line message saying what they taught you and that it's still with you.
Send it now, or save it for the right moment.

wordCard.voice: Your chain: the people who taught you, link by link, with you as the next link. In hadith, the chain is the isnad.

orig.note: Arabic: the chain of narrators that carries a hadith.

carryVoice: Keep this one: a link in the chain, with thanks running back up it. Ten of ten for passing it on.
